title: Quantum Encodings, Private Messages, and Communication Complexity
authors: Tom Gur, Miryam Mi-Ying Huang, Er-Cheng Tang
abstract: We study the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE). We establish a bi-directional connection between the QDRE model and the communication complexity model of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), where classical communication is free, and quantum communication is the primary complexity measure. We show the following upper and lower bounds. (1) For every quantum channel mapping $n$ to $m$ qubits, we give a QPSM protocol with quantum communication $m$, using exponential pre-shared entanglement. In particular, constant-output channels have $O(1)$ quantum communication, and classical-output channels require no quantum communication. (2) With $O(n)$ pre-shared entanglement, every one-qubit-output channel has an $O(n)$-quantum-communication QPSM protocol. Conversely, there exists a channel and a constant $c>0$ for which any protocol with at most $cn$ pre-shared entanglement requires $Ω(n)$ quantum communication. (3) In contrast, we identify a structured class of quantum channels, Clifford-induced channels, for which there exist QPSM protocols with $O(n)$ pre-shared entangled qubits and only $O(1)$ quantum communication complexity. Through our connection, we obtain analogous upper and lower bounds on the quantum encoding size of QDRE. Our results show that the amount of pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity.
summary: This work analyzes the resource requirements for quantum data encoding and private quantum communication protocols. It establishes a crucial link between quantum encoding size and communication complexity, showing that pre-shared entanglement plays a central role. The findings are particularly insightful for understanding the limitations and efficiencies of quantum information processing for structured versus general quantum channels.
main_problem: The paper studies the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE) and establishes a deep connection between this model and the communication complexity of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM).
main_result: The required quantum communication complexity and quantum encoding size are critically dependent on the amount of pre-shared entanglement, with structured channels (Clifford-induced) allowing for significantly reduced communication complexity.
method: The authors establish bi-directional connections between the QDRE model and QPSM, utilizing techniques involving teleportation, Pauli operators, and complexity bounding arguments.
model_or_system: The core models are QDREs, which encode quantum circuits, and QPSM protocols, which secure the computation of an arbitrary quantum channel $\Phi$ among multiple parties.
key_observables: Quantum Encoding Size, Quantum Communication Complexity, Pre-shared Entanglement.
important_parameters: The relationship between the required resources (entanglement vs. communication) for general vs. structured quantum channels.
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between general quantum channels and a structured class called Clifford-induced channels, which permits complexity reduction.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Pauli-Port Complementarity Protocol, detailing the steps involving ordinary teleportation and port-based teleportation to achieve privacy.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the models (QDRE and QPSM), then presents general upper and lower bounds for arbitrary channels, followed by specialized results for Clifford-induced channels, and finally derives corollaries for the quantum encoding size.
why_interesting: While focused on complexity theory, the results provide fundamental bounds on how much quantum information needs to be shared or encoded to simulate quantum processes, which underpins quantum network security and computation.
